title: Inside the Broncos’ New Facility — GTD Mindset, New Direction | Orange & Blue Today
text: It’s a fresh Tuesday at training camp, and on Orange & Blue Today, Mase and Cecil break down the brand‑new Broncos facility — the building that symbolizes a new era, a new standard, and a new mission for 2026. Players reported for camp and walked into a completely transformed environment: A new building, a new locker room, a new training facility, and a new direction for a team that came one game short of the Super Bowl last season. Mase was on site, taking in every detail — from the layout to the energy to the way players reacted to their upgraded home. And everywhere you look, one message stands out: GTD — Go The Distance. It’s on the shirts. It’s on the walls. It’s in the mindset. This team knows exactly how close they were last year… and exactly how far they intend to go now. Cecil and Mase dig into how the new facility impacts preparation, culture, recovery, and performance — and whether this GTD mentality can push the Broncos over the top in 2026. 🔥 In this episode: What Mase saw inside the Broncos’ brand‑new facility How the new locker room and training spaces elevate performance Why “GTD” is more than a slogan — it’s the mission How close the Broncos are to finishing the job they started Whether this new direction helps them finally go the distance Drop your take — can the Broncos GTD this season. Smash LIKE, hit SUBSCRIBE, and join us every day on OBT.

title: Broncos IOL Preview — Meinerz’s All‑Pro Dominance, Powers’ Future | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews continue — this time with a deep dive into the interior of the Broncos offensive line, a group that quietly determines how far the offense can go in 2026. At the center of it all is Quinn Meinerz — one of the best guards in football and the tone‑setter for Denver’s run game. The question now: Can Meinerz continue his All‑Pro dominance in 2026. His power, leverage, and consistency make him the anchor of the entire offense. Next to him, Ben Powers enters what might be his final season in Denver. Contract structure, cap realities, and roster planning all point toward 2026 being a crossroads year. Can he deliver one more strong campaign before the team potentially turns the page. And how does the Broncos IOL stack up against the rest of the league. With Meinerz leading the way, Powers still steady, and young depth developing behind them, Denver’s interior line is better than many realize — but still needs to prove it can be elite in pass protection and durable across a full season. This group is critical to Bo Nix’s Year Three jump, Davis Webb’s offensive rhythm, and the overall identity of the team. 🔥 In this episode: How Denver’s IOL compares to the rest of the NFL Why 2026 could be Ben Powers’ final season in orange & blue Whether Quinn Meinerz can sustain All‑Pro dominance What interior stability means for Bo Nix’s growth How the IOL shapes the Broncos’ offensive ceiling Drop your take — is Denver’s interior line good enough to carry this offense to the next level.

title: Broncos TE Preview — Engram’s Breakout & Rookies Joly/Bentley’s Upside | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews continue — and today we dive into one of the most intriguing rooms on the Broncos roster: the tight ends. With Evan Engram stepping into Davis Webb’s QB‑centric offense, the question becomes simple: Is Engram finally ready for a true breakout season. More motion, more spacing, more designed touches — everything points to Engram being unlocked in ways we haven’t seen yet. Behind him, Adam Trautman remains the steady, reliable glue guy. He’s the trusted blocker, the safety‑valve, the assignment‑sound veteran who keeps the offense on schedule. But the upside in this room comes from the youth movement. Rookie Justin Joly brings fluid athleticism, natural hands, and seam‑stretching ability that could make him one of the steals of the draft. And speaking of steals — did Denver quietly land another one in Dallen Bentley. His toughness, competitiveness, and developmental traits make him a name to watch all camp. This TE room has breakout potential, reliability, and sneaky depth — exactly what Webb’s offense needs. 🔥 In this episode: Why Engram could explode under Davis Webb’s playcalling How Trautman stabilizes the room with veteran consistency Why Justin Joly’s upside is real — and immediate Whether Dallen Bentley is the late‑round steal nobody is talking about How the TE room fits into Bo Nix’s Year Three jump If you’re fired up about this TE room, smash that LIKE button, drop your thoughts in the comments, and SUBSCRIBE for every Broncos position preview.

title: Broncos ILB Preview — Singleton’s Mileage, Strnad’s Ceiling Higher | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews roll on — and today we dig into the Broncos inside linebackers, a room with proven veterans, rising talent, and one rookie who refuses to be overlooked. Alex Singleton remains the heartbeat of the defense, but how much does he have left in the tank. He’s still a tackling machine, still instinctive, still the communicator who keeps the front aligned — but can he maintain that level in 2026 as the mileage adds up. Justin Strnad has been one of Denver’s most underrated defenders. Have we already seen his best, or is there another jump coming now that he’s fully settled into Vance Joseph’s system. His speed and coverage ability remain critical to the ILB room. And then there’s rookie Red Murdock — the seventh‑round steal who keeps showing he’s more than just a developmental pick. Can he get on the field this year. His instincts, tackling, and special‑teams value give him a real shot to carve out snaps earlier than expected. With PJ Locke gone and the defense leaning heavily on communication and versatility, the ILB room’s performance will shape the entire unit. 🔥 In this episode: How much Singleton has left and what his 2026 role looks like Whether Strnad has another level to unlock If Red Murdock can force his way into real playing time How the ILB room fits into Vance Joseph’s turnover‑focused identity Why depth and development matter more than ever at linebacker Drop your take — which ILB surprises in camp and reshapes the rotation.

title: What's the BLUEPRINT for VJ's Broncos Defense To Get More Turnovers? | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews take a big‑picture turn — looking at what Vance Joseph’s defense must do to become the best unit in the NFL. They were already a top‑5 defense last season, but VJ is pushing for more in 2026… and he’s made the goal crystal clear: turnovers. The question is how Denver gets there. Vance Joseph has preached all offseason about increasing takeaways — more interceptions, more forced fumbles, more chaos. But what does that actually look like on the field. How does a top‑5 defense take the next step and become No. 1. To get more interceptions, Denver needs tighter spacing, better route anticipation, and more pressure‑driven throws. Young players like Jonah Elliss, Troy Franklin, and Talanoa Hufanga all play roles in creating those turnover windows. To force more fumbles, the Broncos must lean into their physical identity — attacking the ball, finishing low, and swarming runners with multiple tacklers. VJ wants violence at the point of contact, and this roster is built for it. This defense is already great. The path to becoming the best in the NFL is about finishing plays, stealing possessions, and turning pressure into production. 🔥 In this episode: How VJ’s turnover obsession can elevate Denver to No. 1 What the defense must do to generate more interceptions How they can force more fumbles with technique and aggression Why a top‑5 unit still has room to grow in 2026 Which players must spark the turnover surge Drop your take — can Denver become the NFL’s best defense if they hit VJ’s turnover goals.

title: Broncos Safety Preview — Hufanga’s INT Jump, Jones’ Contract‑Year Surge? | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews continue — this time with a deep dive into the Broncos safeties, a group with star power up top and real questions behind the starters. Talanoa Hufanga was outstanding last season, flying around the field and setting the tone. But dropped interceptions were a problem — so can he turn those near‑misses into game‑changing turnovers in 2026. If he cleans that up, he becomes one of the league’s most dangerous ballhawks. Brandon Jones enters a contract year, and history says players in his situation often explode. Does he ball out of control and earn a new deal. His versatility and physicality make him a perfect fit for Vance Joseph’s turnover‑focused defense. Behind them, things get interesting. With PJ Locke gone, Denver must find out whether JL Skinner or Devon Key can provide starting‑quality play — the kind Locke delivered when called upon. Training camp and preseason will determine whether the Broncos have hidden gems… or a depth concern. 🔥 In this episode: Why Hufanga is primed for more interceptions in 2026 How Brandon Jones’ contract year could fuel a breakout Whether JL Skinner or Devon Key can replace PJ Locke’s reliability If safety depth is a real concern entering camp How the safety room fits into Vance Joseph’s turnover‑driven identity Drop your take — is Denver’s safety depth quietly strong, or a real question mark heading into camp.

title: I Watched Every Bo Nix Deep Throw — What the Film Really Shows About His Game | Orange & Blue Today
text: On today’s Orange & Blue Today, Andrew Mason and Cecil Lammey break down Cecil’s full deep‑ball study: He watched every single Bo Nix throw over 20 yards from the 2025 season to get a true feel for how Denver’s QB has grown as a downfield passer. The film shows a very different story than the national narrative. Bo Nix has no problem throwing deep, even under pressure — he stands tall, keeps his base, and delivers with confidence. But what does he still need to work on. What does the tape reveal about his timing, ball placement, receiver chemistry, and how Sean Payton’s structure helped (and sometimes limited) the deep game. Cecil breaks down the hits, the misses, the near‑misses, and the throws that show Nix’s next level is already forming. 🔥 In this episode: What the film really shows about Nix’s deep‑ball growth Why pressure doesn’t faze him on downfield attempts What mechanical tweaks could boost his consistency How receiver separation and tracking impacted the results What Nix must refine to unlock even more explosive plays Drop your take — is Nix already a better deep passer than people think.

title: Special Teams Preview — Lutz Elite, Crawshaw’s Threat & Mims the All‑Pro KR/PR | Orange & Blue Today
text: Our Orange & Blue Today position previews roll on — and today we spotlight the Broncos special teams, a unit with legitimate star power at all three phases. Will Lutz remains one of the league’s most reliable kickers. His consistency, range, and clutch production give Denver a scoring advantage few teams can match. If the offense stalls, Lutz still turns drives into points. Second‑year punter Jeremy Crawshaw had a fantastic rookie season — booming punts, elite hang time, and directional control that flipped fields all year. The question now: Is Crawshaw already one of the most dangerous punters in the NFL. All signs point to yes. And then there’s Marvin Mims — an All‑Pro returner who gives Denver a weapon most teams simply don’t have. His explosiveness changes games, shifts momentum, and forces opponents to rethink their coverage strategy. This special teams unit isn’t just solid — it’s a difference‑maker. 🔥 In this episode: Why Will Lutz remains one of the NFL’s best kickers How Jeremy Crawshaw could become a top‑tier punter in Year 2 Why Marvin Mims is a true All‑Pro weapon in the return game How special teams can swing close games for Denver in 2026 What the trio of Lutz, Crawshaw, and Mims means for field position and scoring Drop your take — is this the best special teams trio Denver has had in a decade.
